title: The Metropolis Engine: Mechanics & Calibration
text:
The Four Steps of Metropolis-Hastings
The power of Markov Chain Monte Carlo lies in its simplicity. Rather than solving a high-dimensional integral analytically, the algorithm samples from an unnormalized probability density through four iterative steps:

Propose a Candidate Move: Given current state ‭\(\theta^{(t)}\)‬, sample a candidate coordinate ‭\(\theta^*\)‬ from a symmetric proposal distribution:

‭\[\theta^* \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\theta^{(t)}, \sigma_{\epsilon}^2 \mathbf{I}\right)\]‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬

Evaluate the Hastings Acceptance Ratio (‭\(\alpha\)‬): Compare the likelihood of the candidate position to the current position:

‭\[\alpha = \min\left(1, \frac{p(\theta^*)}{p(\theta^{(t)})}\right)\]‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬
In practice, this is evaluated in log-space to prevent numerical underflow:
‭\[\log \alpha = \min\left(0, \log p(\theta^*) - \log p(\theta^{(t)})\right)\]‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬

The Acceptance Decision (Ergodic Coin Flip): Draw a uniform random scalar ‭\(u \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\)‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬. If ‭\(\log u < \log \alpha\)‬‭‬‭‬‭‬, the proposal is accepted:

‭\[\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^*\]‬‭‬
Otherwise, the proposal is rejected, and the chain remains in place:
‭\[\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)}\]‬‭‬

Iterate: Repeating this rule ensures that the empirical frequency of visits converges asymptotically to the true posterior distribution ‭\(p(\theta \mid \mathcal{D})\)‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬.



The Complete Engine in Pure R
Below is the entire algorithm implemented from first principles. There are no black-box packages or opaque wrappers:


Code
run_metropolis <- function(target_log_posterior, initial_theta, iterations = 2000, proposal_sd = 0.05) {
  d <- length(initial_theta)
  theta_current <- initial_theta
  log_p_current <- target_log_posterior(theta_current)

  draws_mat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = iterations, ncol = d)
  accepted  <- logical(iterations)

  for (t in 1:iterations) {
    # 1. Propose candidate jump
    theta_candidate <- rnorm(d, mean = theta_current, sd = proposal_sd)
    log_p_candidate <- target_log_posterior(theta_candidate)

    # 2. Acceptance ratio in log-space
    log_alpha <- log_p_candidate - log_p_current

    # 3. Accept / Reject coin flip
    if (!is.na(log_alpha) && log(runif(1)) < log_alpha) {
      theta_current <- theta_candidate
      log_p_current <- log_p_candidate
      accepted[t]   <- TRUE
    } else {
      accepted[t]   <- FALSE
    }
    draws_mat[t, ] <- theta_current
  }
  
  list(draws = draws_mat, acceptance_rate = mean(accepted))
}




The Goldilocks Dilemma: Tuning Proposal Step Size
The primary operational lever in Random-Walk Metropolis is the proposal standard deviation (‭\(\sigma_{\epsilon}\)‬). Tuning this parameter balances exploration speed against rejection frequency:





Figure 1: Trace plots illustrating the impact of proposal step size on chain mixing and acceptance.






Diagnosing the Three Regimes

Too Timid (‭\(\sigma_{\epsilon} = 0.03\)‬‭‬): Almost every candidate jump is accepted because candidate points sit virtually on top of the current state. However, the chain behaves like slow diffusion—it takes tens of thousands of steps to cross the parameter distribution.
Too Aggressive (‭\(\sigma_{\epsilon} = 3.20\)‬‭‬): The sampler proposes large leaps that consistently land in low-probability regions, causing over 90% of moves to be rejected. The trace plot displays severe horizontal flatlines (“freezing”).
Calibrated (‭\(\sigma_{\epsilon} = 1.20\)‬‭‬): The chain maintains a healthy acceptance rate (~25% to 35%), rapidly mixing across the distribution and generating near-independent parameter draws.

In Portfolio Risk Model, we scale this engine to the full 10-asset risk factor distribution.

title: Audit & Diagnostics
text:
Code
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(gt)
library(reactable)
library(scales)
library(tidyverse)

source("R/metropolis_sampler.R")
source("R/risk_functions.R")
source("R/plots.R")

# 1. Ingest fixture and run two independent chains to test mixing
model_fixture <- build_risk_target("data/synthetic_returns.csv")
d <- model_fixture$d
asset_names <- model_fixture$asset_names

init_theta1 <- rep(0, d)
names(init_theta1) <- asset_names

init_theta2 <- rep(0.001, d)
names(init_theta2) <- asset_names

chain1 <- run_metropolis(
  target_log_posterior = model_fixture$target_fn,
  initial_theta = init_theta1,
  iterations = 3000,
  proposal_sd = 0.00032,
  seed = 42
)

chain2 <- run_metropolis(
  target_log_posterior = model_fixture$target_fn,
  initial_theta = init_theta2,
  iterations = 3000,
  proposal_sd = 0.00032,
  seed = 99
)

# Burn-in discard (first 500 draws)
draws1_clean <- chain1$draws %>% slice_tail(n = 2500)
draws2_clean <- chain2$draws %>% slice_tail(n = 2500)

# 2. Compute Robust Effective Sample Size (ESS) using Geyer's initial sequence estimator
ess_tech  <- compute_ess_robust(draws1_clean$Tech_Growth)
ess_treas <- compute_ess_robust(draws1_clean$US_Treas_10Y)
ess_large <- compute_ess_robust(draws1_clean$US_LargeCap)

# Diagnostic inline variables
txt_acc_c1   <- sprintf("%.1f%%", chain1$acceptance_rate * 100)
txt_acc_c2   <- sprintf("%.1f%%", chain2$acceptance_rate * 100)
txt_ess_tech <- comma(ess_tech)
txt_n_draws  <- comma(nrow(draws1_clean))



Introduction
In institutional risk management, stochastic simulation models must be transparent and auditable. When using Markov Chain Monte Carlo to evaluate high-dimensional portfolio distributions, point estimates alone are insufficient. Because MCMC generates a sequence of dependent parameter proposals rather than independent samples, model validation requires empirical verification of convergence, parameter space exploration, and statistical sample efficiency.
This audit page examines the algorithmic health checks for the 10-dimensional Gaussian random walk. We evaluate multi-chain convergence, measure autocorrelation decay across factor lags, and apply Geyer’s initial sequence estimator to compute robust Effective Sample Size (ESS). This diagnostic audit outlines both the utility of Random-Walk Metropolis and the operational limitations encountered when isotropic proposals are applied to correlated factor distributions.


Dataset Architecture & Methodological Rationale
The analysis utilizes a fixed synthetic fixture of 250 trading days across 10 correlated asset classes (data/synthetic_returns.csv), generated from a known multivariate normal distribution ‭\(\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \mathbf{\Sigma})\)‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬ calibrated to realistic risk levels: annualized returns between 3.5% and 11.0%, volatilities between 8.0% and 26.0%, and correlations from -0.30 to +0.78.
Using a synthetic baseline provides a controlled ground truth. In empirical market feeds, true data-generating distributions are obscured by regime shifts, structural breaks, and survivorship bias. By defining a synthetic population, we establish an explicit benchmark to test whether the sampler recovers sample parameters. Evaluating 10 factors illustrates the scaling challenge where uniform grid search (‭\(10^{10}\)‬ points) becomes computationally impractical, while 250 observations preserve realistic parameter standard errors for downside modeling.


Code
synthetic_data_returns <- as_tibble(read_csv("data/synthetic_returns.csv", show_col_types = FALSE))

reactable(synthetic_data_returns,
  defaultPageSize = 10,
  highlight   = TRUE,
  striped     = TRUE,
  resizable   = TRUE,
  defaultColDef = colDef(
    align = "left",
    format = colFormat(digits = 7),
    width = 110
  ),
  columns = list(
    trading_day = colDef(align = "center", format = colFormat(digits = 0))
  ),
  class = ".react_table",
  theme = reactableTheme(
    borderColor = "#dfe2e5",
    stripedColor = "#f6f8fa",
    style = list(fontSize = "13px", fontFamily = "Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif"),
    searchInputStyle = list(width = "100%")
  )
)








The Diagnostic Framework
In quantitative validation workflows, evaluating an MCMC sampler involves three core criteria: 1. Stationarity: The chain has converged to the target distribution and is invariant to initialization coordinates. 2. Mixing Across Dimensions: The chain traverses parameter space without prolonged freezing or sluggish diffusion. 3. Effective Sample Size (ESS): Autocorrelation decays rapidly enough to provide sufficient independent information for quantile estimation (Vehtari et al., 2021).


Multi-Chain Mixing Verification
To evaluate convergence, two independent chains are tracked from distinct initialization vectors (‭\(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(0)}_1 = \mathbf{0}\)‬‭‬ vs. ‭\(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(0)}_2 = 0.001 \cdot \mathbf{1}\)‬‭‬‭‬).


Code
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8

trace_df <- bind_rows(
  chain1$draws %>% select(iteration, Tech_Growth) %>% mutate(Chain = "Chain 1 (Seed 42)"),
  chain2$draws %>% select(iteration, Tech_Growth) %>% mutate(Chain = "Chain 2 (Seed 99)")
)

ggplot(trace_df, aes(x = iteration, y = Tech_Growth, color = Chain)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.75, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 500, linetype = "dashed", color = "#c0392b", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 520, y = max(trace_df$Tech_Growth) * 0.9, label = "End of Burn-In (500)", fontface = "bold", color = "#c0392b", hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#1b4f72", "#e67e22")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  labs(
    title = "Multi-Chain Stationarity Diagnostic: Tech Growth Exposure",
    subtitle = "Both chains navigate into the stationary posterior distribution",
    x = "Iteration Step",
    y = "Daily Expected Return",
    color = "Sampler Execution"
  ) +
  theme_mcmc()





Figure 1: Two independent MCMC chains tracking Tech Growth expected returns




Diagnostic Review: Multi-Chain Trace

Stationary Overlap: Discarding the first 500 iterations eliminates initial burn-in, after which both chains traverse the same posterior band.
Initialization Distance Note: The initialization vectors (‭\(\mathbf{0}\)‬ vs. ‭\(0.001 \cdot \mathbf{1}\)‬‭‬) differ by approximately 25 basis points annualized. While this demonstrates local convergence into the posterior mode, formal model validation typically tests widely separated, overdispersed starting values (e.g., ‭\(\pm 3 \cdot \text{SE}\)‬‭‬) across 4 or more chains to confirm mixing across distant regions of parameter space.




Autocorrelation Decay Analysis
Because Metropolis-Hastings operates via local proposals, consecutive draws exhibit positive serial dependence.


Code
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8

calc_acf_df <- function(vec, factor_name, max_lag = 35) {
  res <- acf(vec, lag.max = max_lag, plot = FALSE)
  tibble(
    lag = as.numeric(res$lag),
    autocorrelation = as.numeric(res$acf),
    factor = factor_name
  )
}

acf_combined <- bind_rows(
  calc_acf_df(draws1_clean$Tech_Growth, "Tech Growth"),
  calc_acf_df(draws1_clean$US_Treas_10Y, "US Treasuries (10Y)"),
  calc_acf_df(draws1_clean$US_LargeCap, "US Large Cap")
)

ggplot(acf_combined, aes(x = lag, y = autocorrelation, fill = factor)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.10, linetype = "dashed", color = "#7f8c8d") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2c3e50", "#2980b9", "#27ae60")) +
  labs(
    title = "Autocorrelation Decay by Factor",
    subtitle = "Autocorrelation decay profiles highlight the impact of isotropic proposal scaling on correlated parameters",
    x = "Lag Step",
    y = "Autocorrelation Coefficient",
    fill = "Risk Factor"
  ) +
  theme_mcmc()





Figure 2: Autocorrelation decay across consecutive MCMC lags for selected portfolio risk factors




Diagnostic Analysis: The Proposal-Geometry Mismatch
The autocorrelation profiles highlight an operational challenge when using an unscaled, isotropic proposal (‭\(\sigma_\epsilon \mathbf{I}\)‬‭‬) across correlated dimensions:

Treasuries (10Y): Autocorrelation decays quickly, dropping below 0.50 by lag 7 and reaching baseline levels near lag 20. With low return volatility (8%), the parameter space is compact.
Equity Beta (Tech Growth): Autocorrelation exhibits high persistence, remaining around 0.65 at lag 35. Because the scalar proposal step (‭\(\sigma_\epsilon = 0.00032\)‬‭‬) is applied identically across all dimensions, it does not account for the differing scales (Treasuries ‭\(\text{SE} \approx 0.03\%\)‬‭‬‭‬ vs. Tech ‭\(\text{SE} \approx 0.10\%\)‬‭‬‭‬) or the correlated geometry of the target density. As a result, the chain traverses the principal variance axes slowly, leading to persistent serial correlation.




Robust Effective Sample Size (ESS) Audit
To avoid truncation bias in persistent chains, Effective Sample Size is computed using Geyer’s initial sequence estimator across all post-burn draws:


Code
tibble(
  Asset_Class = c("Equity Beta (Tech Growth)", "Duration Hedge (10Y Treasuries)", "Core Market (US Large Cap)"),
  Total_Post_Burn_Draws = rep(nrow(draws1_clean), 3),
  Effective_Sample_Size = c(ess_tech, ess_treas, ess_large),
  Sampling_Efficiency = c(ess_tech, ess_treas, ess_large) / nrow(draws1_clean),
  Autocorrelation_Lag10 = c(
    acf(draws1_clean$Tech_Growth, plot = FALSE)$acf[11],
    acf(draws1_clean$US_Treas_10Y, plot = FALSE)$acf[11],
    acf(draws1_clean$US_LargeCap, plot = FALSE)$acf[11]
  )
) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**MCMC Chain Efficiency & Effective Sample Size Audit**"),
    subtitle = "Robust Geyer initial-sequence evaluation of chain correlation and sampling capacity"
  ) %>%

Model Validation Findings
A model validation review of the ESS diagnostics yields three key takeaways:
1 Sampling Efficiency Reflects Correlation Drag: Out of 2,500 post-burn iterations, Tech Growth yields 19 effective independent draws—a sampling efficiency of approximately 1.5% to 2.0%. While the acceptance rate of 28.9% falls within standard aggregate ranges, the chain experiences high serial correlation due to isotropic proposal variance.  2. Quantile Precision Considerations: Established Bayesian validation standards (Vehtari et al., 2021) recommend an ESS of at least 300 to 400 draws to produce stable tail quantiles and bound Monte Carlo standard error. While an ESS of ‭\(\approx 39\text{--}82\)‬‭‬‭‬ draws is sufficient to estimate the posterior mean vector, downstream tail risk quantiles (such as 95% VaR and Expected Shortfall credible intervals) retain non-trivial Monte Carlo variance.  3. Paths to Algorithmic Improvement: This diagnostic demonstrates the trade-offs of first-principles isotropic Random-Walk Metropolis. In production risk environments, proposal efficiency can be improved by:

Proposal Covariance Preconditioning: Scaling jumps using the empirical covariance matrix ‭\(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{prop}} = \frac{2.38^2}{d} \hat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{\text{post}}\)‬‭‬‭‬ (Roberts & Rosenthal, 2001).
Adaptive Sampling: Implementing adaptive Metropolis algorithms to dynamically learn posterior geometry.
Gradient-Based Methods: Using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) or NUTS to navigate high-dimensional curvature efficiently.

title: 10-Factor Portfolio Risk & Tail Estimation
text:
Introduction
This chapter transitions from two-dimensional toy mechanics to a multi-asset portfolio comprising ten correlated risk factor exposures—spanning core equity betas, corporate credit carry, duration hedges, and commodities.
To provide a mathematically rigorous audit baseline, we formulate a Bayesian return model with a known closed-form solution. We model daily returns as multivariate normal \(\mathbf{R} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \mathbf{\Sigma})\) with a diffuse Gaussian prior on the mean vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, 10^3 \mathbf{I})\) and condition the covariance matrix on the empirical sample estimate \(\mathbf{\Sigma} = \hat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{\text{emp}}\). Under this conjugate structure, the joint posterior distribution of expected returns is analytically known: \[\boldsymbol{\mu} \mid \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{\Sigma} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\bar{\mathbf{x}}, \frac{1}{n} \mathbf{\Sigma}\right)\]
While a closed-form solution exists for this specific Gaussian model, using it as our target allows us to directly benchmark MCMC performance. We can compare the empirical draws, standard errors, and credible intervals from our first-principles Metropolis sampler directly against the analytical truth.


Code
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

library(dplyr)
library(gt)
library(scales)
library(ggplot2)

source("R/metropolis_sampler.R")
source("R/risk_functions.R")
source("R/plots.R")

# 1. Ingest synthetic book fixture and build log-posterior
model_fixture <- build_risk_target("data/synthetic_returns.csv")

# 2. Run 10-dimensional MCMC chain
init_theta <- rep(0, model_fixture$d)
names(init_theta) <- model_fixture$asset_names

chain_10d <- run_metropolis(
  target_log_posterior = model_fixture$target_fn,
  initial_theta = init_theta,
  iterations = 3000,
  proposal_sd = 0.00032,
  seed = 42
)

# 3. Discard first 500 draws as burn-in
post_burn_draws <- chain_10d$draws %>% slice_tail(n = 2500)

# 4. Tail risk evaluation across equal-weighted portfolio
weights_eq <- rep(0.10, 10)
risk_table <- evaluate_portfolio_tail_risk(
  draws_df = post_burn_draws,
  weights = weights_eq,
  cov_mat = model_fixture$cov_emp,
  alpha = 0.95
)

# 5. Pre-formatted text variables for dynamic inline reporting

Context: Isolating Parameter Risk in the Mean Vector
Because the return distribution is modeled as multivariate normal and ‭\(\mathbf{\Sigma}\)‬ is fixed at the sample estimate, the portfolio tail metrics reflect the properties of Gaussian loss distributions under estimation uncertainty:

Mean Uncertainty Bounds (‭\(\text{VaR}_{95\%}\)‬): For an equal-weighted portfolio, parametric Value at Risk is governed by ‭\(\text{VaR}_{95\%} \approx -\mathbf{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu} + 1.645 \cdot \sigma_p\)‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬. Because covariance is held constant, the 12 basis point spread between the 5th and 95th percentiles (‭\(0.99\%\)‬‭‬ to ‭\(1.11\%\)‬‭‬) reflects the estimation uncertainty of the portfolio mean alone (‭\(\pm 1.645 \cdot \sigma_p / \sqrt{n}\)‬‭‬‭‬), setting aside covariance uncertainty.
Expected Shortfall Ratio (‭\(\text{ES}_{95\%}\)‬): The ratio of Expected Shortfall to Value at Risk (‭\(1.33\% / 1.05\% \approx 1.27\)‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬ ‭‬) reflects standard Gaussian tail expectation constants (‭\(\approx 2.063 / 1.645\)‬‭‬), adjusted for the portfolio drift. Under a normal likelihood, this metric captures linear downside expectation rather than excess kurtosis or heavy-tailed structural shocks.

# 1. Ingest fixture and run two independent chains to test mixing
model_fixture <- build_risk_target("data/synthetic_returns.csv")
d <- model_fixture$d
asset_names <- model_fixture$asset_names

init_theta1 <- rep(0, d)
names(init_theta1) <- asset_names

init_theta2 <- rep(0.001, d)
names(init_theta2) <- asset_names

chain1 <- run_metropolis(
  target_log_posterior = model_fixture$target_fn,
  initial_theta = init_theta1,
  iterations = 3000,
  proposal_sd = 0.00032,
  seed = 42
)

chain2 <- run_metropolis(
  target_log_posterior = model_fixture$target_fn,
  initial_theta = init_theta2,
  iterations = 3000,
  proposal_sd = 0.00032,
  seed = 99
)

# Burn-in discard (first 500 draws)
draws1_clean <- chain1$draws %>% slice_tail(n = 2500)
draws2_clean <- chain2$draws %>% slice_tail(n = 2500)

# 2. Compute Effective Sample Size (ESS) Approximation
# ESS = N / (1 + 2 * sum(rho_k))
compute_ess <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  acf_vals <- acf(x, plot = FALSE, lag.max = 40)$acf[-1]
  # Sum positive autocorrelations
  pos_acf <- acf_vals[acf_vals > 0]
  act <- 1 + 2 * sum(pos_acf)
  round(n / act)
}

ess_tech  <- compute_ess(draws1_clean$Tech_Growth)
ess_treas <- compute_ess(draws1_clean$US_Treas_10Y)
ess_large <- compute_ess(draws1_clean$US_LargeCap)

# Diagnostic inline variables
txt_acc_c1   <- sprintf("%.1f%%", chain1$acceptance_rate * 100)
txt_acc_c2   <- sprintf("%.1f%%", chain2$acceptance_rate * 100)
txt_ess_tech <- comma(ess_tech)
txt_n_draws  <- comma(nrow(draws1_clean))



Introduction
In risk management and quantitative finance, it is important that complex models are transparent and can be verified. When using Markov Chain Monte Carlo to assess portfolio tail risk, it is not enough to just get reasonable downside estimates. Since MCMC creates a sequence of dependent parameter proposals instead of independent samples, risk leaders and model validators need clear evidence that the simulation has reached the true stationary distribution, has mixed well across the parameter space, and has enough statistical power.
This audit page sets out the rules and checks that support the whole project. Multi-chain trace diagnostics from different starting points is reviewed, autocorrelation drops off over time are checked, and Effective Sample Size (ESS) is calculated to show that our Metropolis-Hastings sampler gives independent parameter samples for Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES) calculations. With a clear record of the environment, fixed random seeds, and a system dependency check, this section makes sure that all reported results are reproducible, accurate, and ready for audit.


Dataset Architecture & Methodological Rationale
This analysis uses a fixed synthetic dataset of 250 trading days for 10 correlated asset classes data/synthetic_returns.csv. The data comes from a known multivariate normal distribution \(\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \mathbf{\Sigma})\)‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬ , calibrated to match realistic annual risk levels: returns between 3.5% and 11.0%, volatilities from 8.0% to 26.0%, and cross-asset correlations between -0.30 and +0.78. Choosing synthetic data over real market data is intentional. In real financial series, the true data-generating process is hidden and affected by non-stationarity, regime changes, and survivorship bias. By setting a known ground truth, a clear benchmark is created. This lets us directly check, both visually and mathematically, that the Markov chain’s frequencies match the actual parameters, without interference from market noise.
Using ten assets over 250 trading days (about one year) is chosen to show where traditional numerical integration fails, while keeping the model clear and reproducible. The curse of dimensionality grows quickly (‭\(K^D\)‬): a simple 5-asset model can be handled with about 100,000 points, but 10 assets require 10 billion calculations (‭\(10^{10}\)‬), which is too much for standard computers. Increasing to 15 or 25 assets would not change the main point; it would just make the matrices larger, slow down the process, and make the example harder to follow. The 250 daily returns give enough data to build stable covariance estimates and calculate 95% Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES), while still leaving enough uncertainty to show how parameter distributions spread and affect portfolio tail risk.

The Institutional Diagnostic Mandate
In production risk management, Markov Chain Monte Carlo must not be treated as a black-box generator. Because MCMC produces a sequence of dependent draws, risk professionals must run rigorous convergence diagnostics before relying on tail estimates (VaR and Expected Shortfall).
A well-behaved MCMC sampler satisfies three criteria:

Stationarity: The chain has converged to the target joint distribution and is independent of its initialization coordinates.
Effective Mixing: The chain moves freely through the parameter space rather than freezing or wandering slowly.
Decaying Autocorrelation: Successive draws become independent quickly enough to supply sufficient Effective Sample Size (ESS) for downstream quantile calculations.



Multi-Chain Mixing Verification
To verify that the sampler is not trapped on local peaks, two independent chains are initialized from distinct starting vectors (‭\(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(0)}_1 = \mathbf{0}\)‬‭‬ vs. ‭\(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(0)}_2 = 0.001 \cdot \mathbf{1}\)‬‭‬‭‬).

  ) +

Figure 1: Two indedendent MCMC chains tracking Tech Growth expected returns from separate cold starts.




Understanding the Multi-Chain Stationary Diagnostic Plot  The easiest way to is to focus on two things: convergence and intertwining.

Initial Forgetting (Iterations 1–300): On the left side, the two lines begin at different heights. Both colors quickly rise and meet in the same horizontal band, long before the 500-step mark. This shows that the algorithm quickly “forgets” its starting point.
The “Braided Rope” (Iterations 500–3,000): After the red dashed line, the two separate chains fully overlap and move together in the same band, starting at about \(0.15\%\) and \(0.50\%\). Neither chain moves off on its own, gets stuck, or drifts to a different value. If two blindfolded explorers start in different places but end up walking along the same ridge, it shows they are following the real landscape, not just retracing their starting points.

Key Insights  The plot demonstrates why Markov Chain Monte Carlo overcomes the curse of dimensionality where numerical mathematics fails:

No Initial Knowledge Required: The sampler was given zero prior guidance on where the peak probability lay. It started in cold, arbitrary locations and navigated through 10-dimensional space using only local random steps and the Metropolis acceptance rule. Yet, both chains independently discovered the high-density posterior core within a fraction of a second.
Self-Healing Ergodicity: In traditional numerical optimization, algorithms often get trapped in “local traps” (false peaks) and report incorrect answers depending on their initialization. In MCMC, the ability to occasionally accept worse moves guarantees that both chains overcome local obstacles, explore the identical parameter space, and settle into the true stationary distribution.
Institutional Defensibility: For risk and regulatory model-validation teams, this plot provides empirical proof of convergence. Because both chains independently visit the same parameter values with identical frequencies, risk managers can be confident that the downstream Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES) figures reflect genuine market distribution dynamics rather than computational noise.




Autocorrelation Decay Plot
Because MCMC proposes local jumps, consecutive iterations are positively correlated. High autocorrelation reduces the information value of each draw.


Code

#| fig-height: 8

calc_acf_df <- function(vec, factor_name, max_lag = 35) {
  res <- acf(vec, lag.max = max_lag, plot = FALSE)
  tibble(
    lag = as.numeric(res$lag),
    autocorrelation = as.numeric(res$acf),
    factor = factor_name
  )
}

acf_combined <- bind_rows(
  calc_acf_df(draws1_clean$Tech_Growth, "Tech Growth"),
  calc_acf_df(draws1_clean$US_Treas_10Y, "US Treasuries (10Y)"),
  calc_acf_df(draws1_clean$US_LargeCap, "US Large Cap")

  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.10, linetype = "dashed", color = "#7f8c8d") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2c3e50", "#2980b9", "#27ae60")) +
  labs(
    title = "Autocorrelation Decay by Factor",
    subtitle = "Autocorrelation declines rapidly toward zero within 15–20 lags",
    x = "Lag Step",
    y = "Autocorrelation Coefficient",
    fill = "Risk Factor"
  ) +
  theme_mcmc()





Figure 2: Autocorrelation decay across consecutive MCMC lags for selected portfolio risk factors




Understanding the Autocorrelation Decay by Factor Plot  Focus on two things: the slope and the height of the bars.

The Downward Waterfall (Information Shedding): Each factor begins at a height of 1.00 and drops lower as the lag increases. Since Metropolis-Hastings moves in small steps, each step looks similar to the last. The key is how quickly the bars get shorter. If they drop quickly, the sampler quickly loses memory of its past, which helps it explore new areas without bias.
Factor Differences (Treasuries vs. Tech Growth): US Treasuries (green) show the fastest drop, falling below 0.50 by lag 7 and reaching near-baseline by lag 20. Since Treasury duration is tightly limited, the chain covers its full range in just a few steps. Tech Growth (navy) drops more slowly, staying around 0.65 even at lag 35. Because Tech Growth has higher return volatility (26% annualized) and is linked to several other equity factors, it takes more steps to remove serial correlation.

Key Insights  This plot reveals the statistical engine that makes Markov Chain Monte Carlo work in high dimensions:

Uncovering the Real Information Count (ESS): If an analyst runs 2,500 iterations of a model, standard statistics would treat these as 2,500 independent data points. But in a random walk, each step depends on the previous one. This chart helps measure that dependence. By looking at how autocorrelation fades, you can find the Effective Sample Size (ESS). This shows that out of 2,500 draws, hundreds of truly independent samples are obtained, which can used for Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES).
The “Wait, Not a Dead End” Trade-Off: In standard high-dimensional integration, solving 10 dimensions directly is a mathematical wall (10 billion calculations). In MCMC, temporary autocorrelation is accepted in exchange for being able to navigate the space at all. Instead of an impossible integral, the only cost is running a few extra hundred iterations so the chain can shed its memory.
Auditable Governance for Model Validation: Model validation typically committees reject simulation models that suffer from “sticky” or sluggish mixing. This diagnostic provides an empirical audit: it proves the chain is continuously circulating through the 10-dimensional space rather than vibrating in place, ensuring the downside risk percentiles are statistically sound rather than artifacts of sampling drag.




Effective Sample Size (ESS) Summary
Out of 2,500 post-burn iterations, the effective independent sample size for Tech_Growth is 39 draws. In risk management, an ESS above 400 is considered adequate for estimating 95% and 99% portfolio quantiles without excessive variance.

In MCMC, each step depends on the previous one, which creates correlation between nearby draws. title: The Mechanics of Markov Chain Monte Carlo
text:
Introduction
Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is a computational class of algorithms designed to sample from complex, high-dimensional probability distributions when analytical integration is intractable. In portfolio risk management, evaluating joint risk across multiple assets requires characterizing dependent parameters simultaneously—including factor means, volatilities, and cross-asset correlations. For non-standard priors or complex likelihoods, deterministic numerical grid integration scales exponentially with dimension (‭\(K^D\)‬), quickly exceeding practical computational limits. MCMC bypasses deterministic grid mapping by replacing brute-force evaluation with an informed random walk. Guided by transition rules such as the Metropolis-Hastings criterion, the sampler proposes local moves, accepting higher-density coordinates and probabilistically accepting lower-density proposals. Over extended sampling runs, the chain visits parameter states in proportion to their underlying posterior density, mapping the target space without evaluating intractable normalizing constants. In this demonstration, we focus on isolating parameter estimation uncertainty. Using a controlled multivariate Gaussian portfolio framework, we deliberately pair our pure-R Metropolis sampler against a model with an exact analytical solution: ‭\(\boldsymbol{\mu} \mid \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{\Sigma} \sim \mathcal{N}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}, \frac{1}{n}\mathbf{\Sigma})\)‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬‭‬. By holding covariance fixed and evaluating expected returns against this closed-form baseline, we provide an auditable environment to examine convergence, proposal efficiency, and the propagation of parameter uncertainty into Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES).



Plain-Language Translation: How It Works
Imagine being placed on a large, pitch-black terrain with only a small flashlight, tasked with mapping the highest peaks and ridges. You cannot view the entire landscape at once, and pacing every square foot on a rigid grid would take an impractical amount of time. Instead, you take incremental random steps. When a step leads uphill toward higher ground, you take it; when a step heads downhill, you occasionally take it anyway to avoid staying confined to a single minor hill. Because you spend most of your time traversing higher ridges and pass quickly through low valleys, your path naturally traces the contours of the landscape. In financial modeling, algorithms like Markov Chain Monte Carlo deploy this sequential exploration to estimate portfolio risk. Rather than evaluating billions of arbitrary grid points across multiple correlated factors, the sampler concentrates computational effort directly in regions of high probability.



The Dimensional Scaling Challenge
When managing risk across multiple correlated factors—equity betas, credit spreads, duration, and commodities—quantifying joint parameter uncertainty is essential. In low dimensions, deterministic numerical quadratures or grid evaluations are trivial. However, as the parameter count (‭\(D\)‬) increases, Cartesian grid evaluations scale exponentially (‭\(K^D\)‬).

Low-Dimensional Space (‭\(D = 2\)‬‭‬): A coarse 10-point grid requires only ‭\(10^2 = 100\)‬‭‬ function evaluations, making numerical quadratures instantaneous.
Moderate Parameter Space (‭\(D = 10\)‬‭‬): Uniform evaluation along each axis requires ‭\(10^{10}\)‬ calculations (10 billion operations)—creating significant runtime bottlenecks in standard computing environments, whereas stochastic sampling traverses the distribution in seconds.
Full Covariance Horizon (‭\(D = 20\)‬‭‬): Modeling 20 factor means alongside full cross-asset covariances involves ‭\(D + D(D+1)/2 = 230\)‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ distinct parameters. Evaluating such spaces on uniform deterministic grids is computationally intractable, making stochastic simulation essential for non-conjugate structures.



The Random Walk Engine
Markov Chain Monte Carlo navigates probability distributions via sequential, localized transitions:

Propose a Move: The chain samples a candidate coordinate ‭\(\theta^*\)‬ from a proposal distribution centered on the current state ‭\(\theta^{(t)}\)‬.
Evaluate Density Ratio: It computes the target posterior probability ratio between candidate and current locations.
Accept or Reject: Proposals into higher-density regions are accepted; lower-density moves are accepted probabilistically, enabling the chain to explore parameter tails.







NoteThe Metropolis-Hastings Random Walk



Evaluating joint portfolio risk across multiple interdependent assets presents substantial computational complexity when models deviate from simple analytical assumptions. Calculating every joint market permutation across a fine grid requires billions of evaluations, creating an operational bottleneck. The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm resolves this by deploying a sequential “digital scout.” Rather than attempting to evaluate the entire parameter space uniformly, the algorithm takes incremental steps through potential states. If a proposed move discovers a region of higher probability, the chain transitions there; if it steps toward a lower-probability scenario, it still accepts the move occasionally to ensure thorough exploration. Over thousands of iterations, the algorithm visits parameter combinations in proportion to their joint posterior probability. This produces an empirical distribution of parameter uncertainty. For executive decision-makers, this turns otherwise intractable high-dimensional estimation into a practical sampling process, providing an empirical baseline for setting risk capital and stress limits.

Portfolio Risk Model: Sampling the 10-factor posterior under fixed covariance to evaluate Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES) against closed-form benchmarks. library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

source("R/metropolis_sampler.R")
source("R/plots.R")

# Target: Correlated bivariate normal
target_toy <- function(theta) {
  mu <- c(0, 0)
  sigma <- matrix(c(1.0, 0.75, 0.75, 1.0), nrow = 2)
  -0.5 * t(theta - mu) %*% solve(sigma) %*% (theta - mu)
}

# Run 3 chains with varying step sizes to demonstrate tuning
chain_timid <- run_metropolis(target_toy, initial_theta = c(0, 0), iterations = 2000, proposal_sd = 0.03, seed = 101)
chain_wild  <- run_metropolis(target_toy, initial_theta = c(0, 0), iterations = 2000, proposal_sd = 3.20, seed = 101)
chain_tuned <- run_metropolis(target_toy, initial_theta = c(0, 0), iterations = 2000, proposal_sd = 1.20, seed = 101)


he Four Steps of Metropolis-Hastings Rather than solving high-dimensional integrals analytically, the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm generates samples from an unnormalized target density via four iterative steps:  1. Propose a Candidate Move: Given the current state ‭\(\theta^{(t)}\)‬, sample candidate coordinates ‭\(\theta^*\)‬ from a symmetric proposal distribution: ‭\[\theta^* \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\theta^{(t)}, \sigma_{\epsilon}^2 \mathbf{I}\right)\]‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬ 2. Evaluate the Hastings Acceptance Ratio (‭\(\alpha\)‬): Compare target density at the candidate position to the current state: ‭\[\alpha = \min\left(1, \frac{p(\theta^*)}{p(\theta^{(t)})}\right)\]‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬ In practice, this is evaluated in log-space to prevent numerical floating-point underflow: ‭\[\log \alpha = \min\left(0, \log p(\theta^*) - \log p(\theta^{(t)})\right)\]‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ 3. The Acceptance Decision: Draw a uniform scalar ‭\(u \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\)‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬. If ‭\(\log u < \log \alpha\)‬‭‬‭‬‭‬, the candidate is accepted: ‭\[\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^*\]‬‭‬ Otherwise, the candidate is rejected, and the chain remains in place: ‭\[\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)}\]‬‭‬ > Note: While occasionally accepting lower-density moves enables traversal across non-convex surfaces, standard Random-Walk Metropolis remains vulnerable to getting trapped between separated modes on complex, multimodal target surfaces.  4. Iterate: Repeating this transition rule generates an empirical chain whose visited states converge asymptotically to the target posterior distribution ‭\(p(\theta \mid \mathcal{D})\)‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬.


The Complete Engine in Pure R
Below is the complete sampling engine implemented from first principles in base R:


Code
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)

run_metropolis <- function(target_log_posterior,
                           initial_theta,
                           iterations = 5000,
                           proposal_sd = 0.05,
                           seed = NULL) {
  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)

  d <- length(initial_theta)
  theta_current <- initial_theta
  log_p_current <- target_log_posterior(theta_current)

  draws_mat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = iterations, ncol = d)
  accepted  <- logical(iterations)
  log_probs <- numeric(iterations)

  for (t in 1:iterations) {
    if (is.matrix(proposal_sd)) {
      theta_candidate <- MASS::mvrnorm(1, mu = theta_current, Sigma = proposal_sd)
    } else {
      theta_candidate <- rnorm(d, mean = theta_current, sd = proposal_sd)
    }

    log_p_candidate <- target_log_posterior(theta_candidate)
    log_alpha <- log_p_candidate - log_p_current

    if (!is.na(log_alpha) && log(runif(1)) < log_alpha) {
      theta_current <- theta_candidate
      log_p_current <- log_p_candidate
      accepted[t]   <- TRUE
    } else {
      accepted[t]   <- FALSE
    }

    draws_mat[t, ] <- theta_current
    log_probs[t]   <- log_p_current
  }

  param_names <- if (!is.null(names(initial_theta))) {
    names(initial_theta)
  } else {
    paste0("theta_", seq_len(d))
  }

  draws_df <- as_tibble(draws_mat, .name_repair = "minimal")
  colnames(draws_df) <- param_names
  draws_df <- draws_df %>% mutate(iteration = seq_len(iterations))

  diagnostics_df <- tibble(
    iteration = seq_len(iterations),
    accepted = accepted,
    log_posterior = log_probs
  )

  list(
    draws = draws_df,
    acceptance_rate = mean(accepted),
    diagnostics = diagnostics_df,
    dimensions = d,
    proposal_sd = proposal_sd
  )
}





The Step-Size Dilemma: Tuning Proposal Variance
The primary operational lever in Random-Walk Metropolis is the proposal standard deviation (‭\(\sigma_{\epsilon}\)‬). Tuning this parameter governs the trade-off between spatial displacement per jump and proposal rejection frequency:


Code
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10

plot_step_size_comparison(chain_timid, chain_wild, chain_tuned)





Figure 1: Trace plots illustrating the impact of proposal step size on chain mixing and acceptance




Understanding the Trace Plots
The trace panels illustrate the trajectory of parameter ‭\(\theta_1\)‬ over 2,000 steps under three distinct proposal step sizes (‭\(\sigma_\epsilon\)‬), showing how proposal variance governs chain exploration:

Too Timid (‭\(\sigma_{\epsilon} = 0.03\)‬‭‬ — Bottom Panel): Almost every proposal is accepted (98.5% acceptance), but displacement per step is small. The chain wanders sluggishly through diffusion rather than stationary mixing, exhibiting strong positive autocorrelation and requiring extensive iterations to traverse the distribution.
Too Aggressive (‭\(\sigma_{\epsilon} = 3.20\)‬‭‬ — Middle Panel): Large proposal jumps land frequently in low-probability density tails, leading to a rejection rate exceeding 90% (9.9% acceptance). The trace exhibits horizontal flatlines where the state remains frozen across multiple consecutive iterations.
Calibrated (‭\(\sigma_{\epsilon} = 1.20\)‬‭‬ — Top Panel): Jump radius is balanced against target density gradients, achieving an empirical acceptance rate of approximately 34.2% (aligning with theoretical targets of 25% to 40% for low dimensions). The trajectory rapidly oscillates across the distribution center. However, while a calibrated acceptance rate is necessary, it does not alone guarantee rapid autocorrelation decay when applied to high-dimensional, correlated parameters.
